1	---
2	name: horizon
3	description: How to work inside an Archon Horizon workspace — orient from on-disk state, pick the highest-value formalization work, record progress as commits, and coordinate. Load this first; it points to the specialized skills for detail. Editable per workspace.
4	---
5	
6	You are working inside an **Archon Horizon** workspace: a place where AI agents
7	formalize mathematics in Lean 4 across one or more projects. This skill is the
8	map. It is deliberately short and **you can edit it** (it lives at
9	`.claude/skills/horizon/SKILL.md` in this workspace) — tune it to how you want to
10	work. It points to focused skills; load those on demand rather than up front.
11	
12	## You are a team; the workspace is where teams collaborate
13	
14	Think of your session as **one team**: you (the lead) plus the subagents you
15	spawn as your **workers**, with the tools and skills available to you. A
16	`horizon run` is your team working through its task. Other runs are **other
17	teams** working in parallel on the *same shared workspace* — one Lean project set,
18	one roadmap/board, one ledger, one inbox.
19	
20	You do not manage other teams and they do not manage you. You coordinate through
21	**shared state**, not meetings:
22	
23	- **The board (roadmap)** is the shared plan. Keep your items' status/owner/
24	  milestone current so other teams see what you hold and where it's going.
25	- **The inbox** is asynchronous messaging + memory across teams (skill:
26	  `horizon-inbox`): shared notes, per-task private items, and direct messages to
27	  another team.
28	- **Commits** are the durable record; reading recent ledger history tells you what
29	  other teams just produced (skill: `project-git`).
30	
31	Before you start, be aware of who else is live (see "Is another run live" below).
32	A short **synchronizer** digest is printed to stderr at the start of your CLI
33	commands. Its attention order is deliberate: `REQUIRED` active protections,
34	`ACTION` unread conversations, advisory unread inbox, then session/runtime and
35	other live runs. Read it; it is how you stay aware without asking anyone. A new
36	conversation or reply invalidates the digest cache immediately. If stderr is
37	redirected, the same protection/conversation lanes are the first `attention`
38	object in `horizon inbox list --json`.
39	
40	## Orient (pull state, don't assume it)
41	
42	**Start here:** your prompt says nothing about who ran before you. Usually
43	somebody did — often minutes ago, often on this same task, and their report was
44	written for you. Skill: `horizon-start` — one cheap pass that works out which
45	situation you were launched into (fresh run, hand-off from the session that just
46	finished, resume after a crash, or outside a run) and what to read for each.
47	
48	The workspace root is `$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT`; your shell may start in a member
49	project rather than at that root. The absolute path to this skill is
50	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL`. Live state is under
51	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/.archon-horizon/` and the manifest is
52	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/config.yaml`. Read what you need, when you need it — via the
53	`horizon` CLI (invoke it as `"$HORIZON_BIN" …`):
54	
55	- **Roadmap** — YOUR strategy sketch across *all* projects, kept as a nested
56	  outline. `"$HORIZON_BIN" roadmap list` renders the indented tree with per-parent
57	  progress (`active · 3/7 done`); `--focus <id>` shows one subtree, `--max-depth 0`
58	  the top level only. Structure it: nest sub-goals with `--parent`, keep your
59	  item's status/strategy current as you work. It doubles as the **project board**:
60	  set `--owner <team>` (who holds it), `--milestone <label>` (a free grouping tag,
61	  filter with `roadmap list --milestone <label>`), and pin concrete deliverables
62	  with `--pin-commit <sha>`. Roadmap commands print a **warning**
63	  when parent/child statuses disagree (all sub-items done but parent open, or a
64	  done parent with open children) — nothing is auto-corrected; you decide whether
65	  to fix it or leave it (it may be intentional). They also warn when too many
66	  milestones claim simultaneous `active` focus.
67	- **Tasks** — a specific piece of work, usually the one a human launched and is
68	  watching. `"$HORIZON_BIN" task …`. Task commands warn when the open queue grows
69	  beyond the advisory limit or a `running` status looks orphaned.
70	- **Inbox** — how teams talk across sessions and projects. Leave a note for the
71	  next session; read what past ones left. `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox …` (skill:
72	  `horizon-inbox`). Items can be **owned by your task** (private, e.g. your team's
73	  memory) or **shared with everyone** (the default); read-state is per-team, so
74	  `inbox list --mine --unread` is your team's fresh queue, and you can
75	  direct-message another team with `--to task:<id>`. Inbox commands warn when the
76	  open working set—especially `memory` and `info`—needs review.
77	- **Inbox attention order** — before edits, inspect all open `protection` items
78	  (standing constraints, whether read or unread), then open unread
79	  `conversation` items and reply or mark them read. Other kinds are advisory
80	  context. In an agent session an unqualified `inbox list` defaults to open items
81	  and sorts in this order; use an explicit status to audit history.
82	- **Conversation discipline** — use a conversation only when a reply/decision is
83	  expected. Search and reuse an open thread before starting one. Its initiator is
84	  a participant and owns closure: after consuming the answer, add a concise
85	  conclusion if needed and archive the thread. Reply to human-started threads but
86	  leave their closure to the human unless asked otherwise (skill: `horizon-inbox`).
87	- **Blueprint graph** — declaration dependencies and what's proved. `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> …` (skill: `hgraph`).
88	  Each node is also an **hgraph** file with attached comments/reviews —
89	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` ranks what to prove next, and node-scoped failure memory
90	  goes on the node itself (skill: `hgraph`).
91	- **Memory** — durable facts/dead-ends live in the inbox: read with
92	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox list --kind memory --json`, write with
93	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox add --kind memory --to horizon --body …`.
94	- **Usage** — your token/cost consumption this session and run, budget headroom,
95	  and recent rate-limit signals: `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json`. See
96	  "Pace yourself" below for how to act on it.
97	
98	## Your session's identity (environment variables)
99	
100	The harness exports these to every session — read them instead of guessing:
101	
102	| Variable | Meaning |
103	|---|---|
104	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT` | workspace root (use for `--root`-free CLI calls) |
105	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL` | absolute path to this `SKILL.md` (never resolve it relative to the shell cwd) |
106	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_RUN` | run id (e.g. `0163`) |
107	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION` | this session's name (e.g. `0002-horizon-T-1`) |
108	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION_DIR` | this session's directory (transcript, usage.json, report) |
109	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS` | which round this is (0-based) / the run's planned total |
110	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK_TITLE` | the task id / title (full body: `"$HORIZON_BIN" task show "$ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK" --json`) |
111	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_PROJECTS` | comma-separated projects this task spans |
112	| `HORIZON_BIN`, `HORIZON_GIT` | absolute paths to the CLI and the ledger-git wrapper |
113	| `HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR`, `HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE` | the workspace ledger repo + its work tree — `"$HORIZON_GIT" …` is shorthand for `git --git-dir "$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree "$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" …` |
114	
115	## Pace yourself (usage & interruption risk)
116	
117	Sessions end for reasons you don't control: rate limits, usage caps, budgets.
118	The defense is NOT to avoid work — it is to make interruption cheap:
119	
120	- **Commit at every coherent point** (plain git into the ledger, below). If
121	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` shows low budget headroom or recent
122	  `rate_limit`/`usage_limit` signals, commit what you have NOW and prefer
123	  finishing the piece in flight over opening a new front.
124	- If this is the run's **last round** (`ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` + 1 ==
125	  `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS`), leave the workspace hand-off-clean: commit, update
126	  the roadmap/task status, and write the report as if nobody continues today.
127	- Interrupted anyway? Nothing is lost that was committed — the next session
128	  resumes from the ledger (see "Resuming" below).
129	
130	## One-shot discipline (important)
131	
132	This session runs to completion and is **not resumed** — you will not be re-invoked
133	when a background job finishes. So **run work in the foreground and block on it**
134	(builds, checks, subagents). Anything you leave running in the background, or leave
135	uncommitted, may be lost when the session ends. Commit early and often (below).
136	
137	## Pick the highest-value work
138	
139	Read the roadmap and the live Lean state, then commit to the most valuable next
140	piece. A node being large, multi-session, or blocked on missing mathlib
141	infrastructure is **not** a reason to skip it — start it, build the missing
142	lemma/definition yourself as project-local infrastructure, and push it as far as
143	you genuinely can. Prefer ambitious progress over defensive avoidance.
144	
145	If this session was launched on a specific task, make concrete progress on that
146	task's REAL objective — don't preemptively pivot to easy unrelated wins because
147	the objective is large. Leave a concise task comment only for a durable state
148	change or blocker, not every action. You own the task's terminal status (skill:
149	`task-status`): set `--status done` only when the objective is FULLY complete;
150	`blocked`/`failed` if genuinely stuck; set nothing if it's only partly advanced
151	(it returns to the queue).
152	
153	## Fresh-context checkpoints
154	
155	The old Ground pass is no longer a second orchestrator role, but independent
156	review is still part of convergence. Spawn the **`ground`** subagent at these
157	checkpoints:
158	
159	- before marking a multi-step task `done`;
160	- after every two substantive Horizon sessions on a long-running task;
161	- immediately after a strategy pivot, a broad workspace edit, or a surprising
162	  clean/build result.
163	
164	Give it the task/project scope and ask it to inspect the actual ledger diff,
165	blueprint graph, Lean state, roadmap, inbox, and reports with fresh context. It
166	is read-only on source and reports issues/memory; reconcile its findings before
167	continuing. Use **`work-reviewer`** for a narrow diff/proof audit and **`janitor`**
168	when the main concern is workspace hygiene. A one-session task may skip the
169	periodic checkpoint, but must still obtain a fresh-context review before a
170	terminal `done` claim.
171	
172	Schedule upkeep even when the last command did not print a warning. On a
173	multi-session run, dispatch **`janitor` at the start of every second Horizon
174	session** and before the final report; on a one-session task, dispatch it once
175	before claiming completion if the run touched roadmap, task, or inbox state.
176	Record the checkpoint in the report and wait for the helper before continuing.
177	If `janitor` is unavailable, ask **`ground`** for the same hygiene inspection;
178	Ground is read-only, so apply or explicitly record its findings yourself.
179	
180	## Warnings are work
181	
182	Commands report problems for a reason — never scroll past them. `lake build`
183	warnings, `horizon graph sync` warnings, roadmap consistency warnings, deprecation
184	notices from any tool: if your change caused it, **fix it now** (it is part of
185	the task); if it's pre-existing or caused by the tool/command itself, don't
186	silently ignore it — record it as a memory item, file an inbox `issue`, or
187	address it `--to human` when a human decision is needed. A warning that
188	survives your session should be one you *chose* to leave, with a trace saying
189	why.
190	
191	Collection-health warnings are a dispatch trigger, not background noise. When
192	`inbox`, `roadmap`, or `task` reports an overloaded queue, stale running item,
193	or status mismatch, pause the proof loop and spawn **`janitor`** with the
194	workspace scope. Wait for it, reconcile its report, rerun the command, and
195	record any warning that remains intentionally. Do this at most once for the
196	same warning in a session; a persistent warning still needs a report or inbox
197	issue rather than repeated no-op calls.
198	
199	## Do the work (Lean)
200	
201	For any Lean edit, load `lean-check` before touching the file and follow its
202	required LSP loop: query the target with `lean_diagnostic_messages` or
203	`lean_goal` before the first edit and after each subsequent edit. Keep `lake
204	build` for the final session boundary or a specifically required kernel check;
205	LSP is enough between edits and proof obligations. Use the narrowest `lake env
206	lean` fallback when LSP is unavailable, and do not duplicate that check when the
207	configured final build covers the same files.
208	
209	**Do not `grep` for a lemma.** Grep matches names you already guessed; it cannot
210	find the lemma whose name you don't know, and that is the one that costs you an
211	afternoon. This workspace indexes every declaration in every project *and* in
212	mathlib — query it:
213	
214	| You want | Use | Not |
215	|---|---|---|
216	| "does this lemma exist, anywhere?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" search "<words or name>" --json` | `grep -r` |
217	| "what's the lemma for this *statement*?" | LSP `lean_leansearch` (natural language) | guessing names |
218	| "what matches this *type*?" | LSP `lean_loogle` (`Nat → ?a → ?a`) | `grep` |
219	| "does something in scope close this goal?" | LSP `lean_local_search` / `lean_hover_info` | reading files |
220	| "what should I prove next?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` (ranked) | scanning the blueprint |
221	| "what does this node depend on / block?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> get label:<id>` | reading imports |
222	| "is the proof right?" | `lake env lean <file>` (narrowest faithful check) | `lean_diagnostic_messages` alone |
223	
224	`"$HORIZON_BIN" search` covers **your projects and mathlib together**, which is
225	its whole point: the premise you need is usually already in mathlib under a name
226	you would never have grepped for. One query costs a second; re-proving an
227	existing lemma costs a session. If it reports a library as unindexed, fix that
228	first (`lake build`, then `"$HORIZON_BIN" search --reindex`) rather than falling
229	back to grep.
230	
231	Grep is still the right tool for what it *is* good at: finding a known string, a
232	specific file, or every call site of a name you already have.
233	
234	- Search before proving — the lemma may already exist. Skill: `leansearch`.
235	- Use the **Lean LSP MCP** for tight proof feedback, then verify with the narrowest
236	  faithful `lake` / `lake env lean` check. Skill: `lean-check`.
237	- Use the DAG to choose and scope work, not just to report it. Skill: `hgraph`.
238	- When editing blueprint material, follow the house format. Skill: `blueprint-conventions`.
239	  The blueprint is timeless mathematics, never a formalization journal. Put Lean
240	  implementation notes, failed tactics, and declaration-specific progress on the
241	  corresponding hgraph node with `graph add comment`; do not insert
242	  "Formalization note" paragraphs into blueprint `.tex` files.
243	
244	## Read the other projects
245	
246	They are in this workspace for a reason: the same lemma, pattern, or dead end has
247	often already been worked out next door. `"$HORIZON_BIN" search` spans **all**
248	projects — an existing construction in another project is a lead, whether you
249	import it, copy the approach, or read its blueprint. `references/` holds the
250	original sources (skill: `references`). Staying inside your own project because
251	the task named it is how the workspace re-derives the same thing three times.
252	
253	## Delegating beyond your team (ask permission first)
254	
255	Your normal way to parallelize is **within** your team: spawn subagents/workers
256	(skill: `subagents`) and dispatch scoped work to them in the foreground. That
257	needs no permission.
258	
259	Launching work **outside** your team — creating new tasks for other teams, or
260	spawning a whole new `horizon run` — is different: it spends the user's compute
261	and accounts, so it is **off by default**. Before you even consider it, read the
262	standing consent: `"$HORIZON_BIN" permissions --json`. It reports
263	`allow_launch_tasks`, `allow_launch_runs`, `max_parallel_sessions`, any declared
264	`accounts`, and free-form notes the user left (e.g. which account to prefer, when
265	limits reset). If both `allow_*` are false (the default), **do not** create tasks
266	or launch runs on the user's behalf — instead leave an inbox item `--to human`
267	proposing the delegation and why. Only when a flag is enabled may you act within
268	its stated caps, and follow the account/usage notes the user recorded.
269	
270	## Record progress = commit (this is how progress is read)
271	
272	Your commits — message + diff — are the durable record of what you did; the
273	dashboard reads progress from them. Commit coherent progress yourself with plain
274	`git` into the workspace ledger. Skill: `project-git` (use `"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m …`
275	or the explicit `--git-dir/--work-tree` form; provenance trailers are auto-stamped).
276	
277	Write **semantic, math-first** messages that say what you proved/built. Prefer
278	staging explicit files over `add -A`. Beyond commits:
279	
280	- Commit after each independently useful verified proof, file, or bounded tooling
281	  change; commit before long builds/reviews and before expanding scope. Multi-hour
282	  implementation sessions normally produce several commits.
283	- Never end a session with durable authored changes after the last commit. The
284	  lifecycle hook gives a compact checkpoint reminder and may pause Stop when it
285	  observed a file mutation after the last commit.
286	- Keep operational prose as a delta. Task/roadmap/inbox comments default to one
287	  sentence or at most three bullets: conclusion, evidence, next action. Do not
288	  copy the report, commit summary, or thread history into them.
289	
290	- Update the **roadmap** with coarse status/strategy (not a re-narration of the diff).
291	- Use the **inbox** to hand off to the next/other sessions; record durable dead-ends
292	  as **memory**.
293	
294	Before your final report, do one boundary-maintenance pass. Re-read the task's
295	`roadmap_refs` and `inbox_refs`; update each roadmap milestone whose status or
296	strategy changed, add a concise mathematical comment for a key advance, and
297	archive or complete open inbox items your work actually resolved. Also scan the
298	remaining open inbox for consumed temporary/info/memory items and archive those
299	that are now stale. Never archive a standing protection merely to make the list
300	shorter. In particular, review every open conversation your task started: archive
301	answered threads and leave a concrete blocker on any that must stay open. This
302	pass is part of completing the work, not optional janitor follow-up.
303	
304	## Resuming after an interruption
305	
306	State lives on disk, so a fresh session (even on another account) continues
307	cheaply. Working out *whether* you're resuming, and what to read if you are, is
308	the `horizon-start` skill — load it at the start of the session. The essentials:
309	
310	- **Why did the last run stop?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` includes a
311	  `paused` field (from `runs/<id>/paused.json`) with the reason (usage limit,
312	  budget, …) and the exact resume command; `recent_failure_reasons` shows
313	  rate-limit signals. A paused/killed run resumes with
314	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" run --resume <id>`.
315	- **What was in flight?** Read recent ledger history (`project-git` skill:
316	  `git log` + `git show` by `Archon-Session` trailer) and the previous
317	  session's transcript/report under `.archon-horizon/runs/`. A horizon session
318	  directory with **no `report.md`** is one that was killed mid-flight.
319	- **Is another run live on this workspace?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" ps` lists runs
320	  holding a process (the ledger is one shared branch — be aware of parallel
321	  writers); it also flags zombie markers and stalled runs. A run registers a
322	  `runs/<id>/process.json` marker (pid/host) at start and removes it on clean
323	  exit; `ps` decides liveness by probing the pid on the local host (a marker whose
324	  pid is dead is a reap-able zombie, a live pid idle for a long time is "stalled").
325	  The synchronizer surfaces the same "other runs live" signal at command start, so
326	  you usually don't need to call `ps` explicitly.
327	
328	## Final report (your last message)
329	
330	Your final message is saved as the session's report — a human or the next
331	session should understand the session from it without opening raw logs.
332	Use only sections that carry information: normally `## Progress`, `## Issues`,
333	`## Why I stopped`, and `## Next`. In `## Progress`, use one inline `-` bullet per file/target,
334	e.g. `- FileA.lean: 4 sorries -> 3; closed the base case.` In `## Why I
335	stopped`, say plainly whether the objective is fully complete, partly advanced,
336	or blocked — and why. Always mention build failures, broken proofs, blocked
337	dependencies, and checks that failed or were not run. If a plausible next
338	action fits in the session's scope, take it before stopping — a clean commit is
339	not by itself a reason to stop. Do not replay the chronological session log.
340	
341	## Cleaning up the work (you decide, via subagents)
342	
343	There is no second orchestrator role running alongside you. *You* are the driver,
344	and the **`ground`** subagent is the scheduled fresh-context checkpoint when the
345	workspace or strategy needs an external view. Available helpers (see the
346	`subagents` skill):
347	
348	- **janitor** — workspace hygiene: roadmap/READMEs concise, inbox from overflowing.
349	- **ground** — workspace-wide strategy, graph, ledger, and convergence review.
350	- **work-reviewer** — fresh-context review of your last work; is it converging?
351	- **blueprint** — Lean ↔ blueprint statement/`\uses` correctness for a scoped slice.
352	- **reference-retriever**, **debug**, **page-transcriber** — as needed.
353	
354	Keep proving; delegate the upkeep.
355

---
name: horizon-start
description: Work out which situation you were launched into — first round of a fresh run, a hand-off from the horizon session that just finished, a resume after a crash or pause, or a session outside any run — and pull exactly the context that situation calls for. Load at the START of a session, before picking up the task.
---

Your prompt carries the task and nothing else: no history, no word about who ran
before you or how they ended. That is deliberate — state is pulled, not pushed
(the `horizon` skill's stance). But it means a session that starts working
immediately is guessing. Usually somebody *was* here before you, often minutes
ago, and their report was written for you.

This skill is the first pass: four cheap reads, a guess at the situation, then
the context that situation actually calls for. Budget a couple of minutes, not a
tenth of the session.

## The four signals

```bash
ls "$ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION_DIR/.."     # sibling sessions in THIS run
"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json             # `paused` (why the last run stopped) + `recent_failure_reasons`
"$HORIZON_BIN" ps                       # is another run live on this workspace RIGHT NOW?
"$HORIZON_GIT" log --oneline -15        # what actually landed recently
```

The sibling listing is the one that decides most of it. A run's sessions look
like:

```
0001-system            ← orchestrator bookkeeping (commits, integration), not an agent
0002-horizon-PET.5     ← a horizon session; meta.json + transcript.jsonl + usage.json
0003-system
0004-horizon-PET.5     ← ...you, probably
```

For any earlier `*-horizon-*` sibling, two files answer everything:

- **`report.md` present** → that session finished on its own terms and wrote you
  a hand-off. **`report.md` absent** → it was killed mid-flight. This is the
  single most informative bit on disk.
- **`meta.json`** → `round`, `task_id`, `status`, `started_at`, `ended_at`,
  `model`. `ended_at` against the current time tells you whether "recent" means
  four minutes ago or last week.

## Which situation am I in?

Work down the list; the first match is your best guess.

**An earlier horizon sibling has no `report.md`** → *resume after a crash or
kill.* Its work is half-done and possibly half-committed. Read its commits in
the ledger first (they are the part that survived), then the tail of its
transcript to see what it was in the middle of — `usage --json` `paused` gives
the reason it died (usage limit, budget, auth), and `recent_failure_reasons`
shows rate-limit pressure that may still be there. Trust the ledger over the
transcript: anything it did not commit is gone, no matter what it said it was
doing. If the dead session shares your `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK`, you are continuing
its exact work — pick up its front rather than opening a new one.

**An earlier horizon sibling has a `report.md`** → *hand-off from the session
that just finished.* The common case. Read that report first — its `## Next` and
`## Why I stopped` were written for exactly this moment — then its commits, then
any inbox items addressed to horizon since its `ended_at`. Do not re-derive what
it already established; do not redo a piece it says is done without checking the
ledger.

**`ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` is `0` and no horizon sibling exists** → *first agent
of the run.* Nobody handed you anything **in this run** — but the workspace is
almost never greenfield. Earlier runs live under `.archon-horizon/runs/`; the
roadmap, the inbox and the ledger carry their conclusions. Skim the roadmap and
recent ledger history before deciding a strategy that a previous run already
tried and rejected.

**`ARCHON_HORIZON_RUN` is unset** → *not launched by the orchestrator* (an
interactive or hand-driven session). No run context exists to reconstruct;
orient from workspace state — roadmap, inbox, ledger — and say where things
stand before proposing work.

for "am I first" — but a resumed run can re-run a round whose session died, so a

check settles it either way. (`ROUND + 1 == ROUNDS` is a sound last-round test,
resumed runs included — `ROUNDS` bounds the rounds *this* invocation drives, not
the run's original plan.)

  Commit in small coherent pieces and expect to see its commits interleaved.
- **Timestamps are context.** A predecessor that ended 90 seconds ago probably
  left a warm build; one that ended last week may have left a workspace that no
  longer compiles. Check rather than assume.

  horizon, and the task's own comments if you share their `task_id`

smarter place than round zero — not to reconstruct everything that ever happened

1	# Concurrent-lane protocol (2026-07-16, from inbox I-0149's incidents — BINDING for parallel agent fleets)
2	
3	Adopted after the 2026-07-16 evening wave's four incidents (I-0149). These rules extend the
4	standing handoff protocol (07-14/14b/15) for any session running two or more lanes in this
5	workspace.
6	
7	## 1. Ledger commits: private index + compare-and-swap (the shared-index race)
8	
9	All lanes commit through one `workspace.git`; concurrent `git add`+`commit` through the
10	SHARED index can interleave and record spurious deletions of another lane's
11	freshly-committed files (happened in `6197c9676`, 862 lines vanished from HEAD, restored
12	byte-identical in `a640fef5b`). Concurrent lanes MUST commit via a private index:
13	
14	```bash
15	cd /home/axel/LeanAlgebraicGeometry-Horizon
16	GD=.archon-horizon/vcs/workspace.git
17	export GIT_INDEX_FILE=$(mktemp)
18	git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. read-tree HEAD
19	git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. add <ONLY your paths…>
20	TREE=$(git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. write-tree)
21	PARENT=$(git --git-dir=$GD rev-parse HEAD)
22	COMMIT=$(git --git-dir=$GD -c user.name="Archon Horizon" -c user.email="archon-horizon@local" \
23	  commit-tree $TREE -p $PARENT -m "<math-first message>
24	
25	Archon-Commit: agent
26	Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>")
27	git --git-dir=$GD update-ref refs/heads/main $COMMIT $PARENT   # CAS: fails if HEAD moved
28	unset GIT_INDEX_FILE
29	```
30	
31	If the `update-ref` CAS fails (HEAD moved), re-read HEAD and repeat — never force.
32	ALWAYS verify afterward: `git --git-dir=$GD show --stat HEAD` must touch only your paths.
33	A single-lane session may keep the plain `add`+`commit` recipe, but must still verify.
34	
35	### 1a. THE RECIPE ABOVE HAS A RACE — read HEAD ONCE, not twice (2026-07-28, run 0072)
36	
37	**As written, the recipe reads `HEAD` twice**: once in `read-tree HEAD`, and again several lines
38	later in `PARENT=$(… rev-parse HEAD)`. If another lane's CAS lands **between those two reads**,
39	your tree is built from the *old* snapshot while your parent is the *new* commit — and
40	`update-ref` **succeeds**, because it only checks that the ref has not moved since `rev-parse`.
41	It never checks that the tree was built from that ref. You publish a stale tree, silently
42	reverting everything that landed in the window.
43	
44	**Measured once, and the measurement is narrow — do not over-read it.** `e964967e8` has parent
45	`a1ef4d59c` and, diffed against *that parent*, deletes 95 lines of
46	`informal/w4-rep-critical-path.md`, 52 of `informal/w5-t4-worksheet.md` and 19 of
47	`Picard/Pic0ChartLocusIsOpen.lean` — exactly the restore `a1ef4d59c` had just performed, undone.
48	Its `read-tree` ran before `a1ef4d59c` landed; its parent was captured after. It staged explicit
49	paths and the pathspec *was* honoured: **the sweep came from the TREE BASE, not the pathspec**,
50	which is why "stage explicit files" is not a defence and why the symptom is indistinguishable
51	from §1b's shared-index staleness.
52	
53	**Two other lanes audited their own CAS commits the same day (fifteen commits between them,
54	recipe verbatim) and found zero reverts.** That is consistent with this: the race only fires when
55	another lane's CAS lands inside your particular window, so clean commits are the expected
56	outcome, not evidence of absence. The discriminating question is not "did my commits look clean"
57	but "was my `read-tree` separated from my `rev-parse` by somebody else's commit". Treat §1a as
58	cheap insurance, not as a diagnosis of every mystery revert — and check §1b too.
59	
60	**The fix is one line — capture the parent BEFORE the tree, and read-tree that sha:**
61	
62	```bash
63	PARENT=$(git --git-dir=$GD rev-parse HEAD)     # ONCE, up front
64	export GIT_INDEX_FILE=$(mktemp)
65	git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. read-tree $PARENT      # not "HEAD"
66	git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. add <ONLY your paths…>
67	TREE=$(git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. write-tree)
68	COMMIT=$(git --git-dir=$GD … commit-tree $TREE -p $PARENT -m "…")
69	git --git-dir=$GD update-ref refs/heads/main $COMMIT $PARENT   # now genuinely atomic
70	```
71	
72	Then a mid-recipe CAS by another lane makes `update-ref` **fail**, you re-read and retry, and the
73	protocol behaves as it was meant to. The verification step ("must touch only your paths") is what
74	catches it after the fact — run it every time, and read the file list, not just the count.

76	### 1b. The CAS recipe leaves the SHARED index permanently stale — this is by design, and it is armed
77	
78	Added 2026-07-27 (run 0048 r5) after this failed a **third** time (`I-0366`: the shared index
79	was pinned to a pre-round-5 snapshot and a bare `git commit` would have deleted
80	`Picard/JacobianDataCharts.lean` and un-rooted it from `AlgebraicJacobian.lean` in one commit).
81	
82	The mechanism is not a bug in anyone's lane, it is the direct consequence of §1: a CAS commit
83	publishes a tree built in a **private** `GIT_INDEX_FILE` and moves the ref with `update-ref`.
84	The **shared** index is never touched, so the moment anybody commits, the shared index still
85	describes the previous HEAD — and `git status` then reports that difference as *staged changes*,
86	including **staged deletions** for any file the commit added. The longer a run goes, the further
87	the shared index drifts behind.
88	
89	Consequences, all three binding:
90	
91	1. **Never run a bare `git commit` (no `-a`, no pathspec) against `workspace.git`.** It publishes
92	   whatever the stale shared index holds, which is a reversion of other lanes' work.
93	2. **Before finishing, check and repair.** `git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. status --porcelain | grep '^D'`
94	   must be empty. If it is not, repair with the **narrowest** form that covers your paths:
95	   `git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. reset -q -- <your project dir>/`. Prefer this to a whole-index
96	   `read-tree HEAD` when another run is live — a full reset can discard the other run's staging.
97	3. **Verify the worktree is the good copy before repairing.** `reset` makes the index match HEAD;
98	   that is only safe once you have confirmed the on-disk file is the one you want
99	   (`diff <(git --git-dir=$GD cat-file -p HEAD:<path>) <path>`).
100	
101	Expect to repeat step 2 more than once in a long session: every CAS commit by any lane re-stales
102	the index, so a repair done early does not stay done.

104	## 2. The lake mutex is a mkdir DIRECTORY lock — never flock a file there
105	
106	`/tmp/claude-1001/ajcr-locks/lake.lock` is acquired by `mkdir` (atomic; a crash leaves a
107	directory that the next holder's timeout logic can reap). It is NOT a flock file: a lane
108	that runs `flock /tmp/claude-1001/ajcr-locks/lake.lock …` creates a plain FILE at the
109	path, and every mkdir-acquire loop then spins forever (this deadlocked all lanes
110	15:18–19:10 on 2026-07-16 until a human deleted it). Acquire pattern:
111	
112	```bash
113	LOCK=/tmp/claude-1001/ajcr-locks/lake.lock
114	while ! mkdir "$LOCK" 2>/dev/null; do
115	  # (a) plain FILE at the path = a flock protocol-violation; reap immediately.
116	  if [ -f "$LOCK" ]; then echo "STALE: plain file at $LOCK (flock violation) — removing" >&2; rm -f "$LOCK"; continue; fi
117	  # (b) orphaned DIRECTORY from a crashed build (rmdir never ran). Reap on proof of death:
118	  if [ -d "$LOCK" ]; then
119	    holder=$(cat "$LOCK/pid" 2>/dev/null)
120	    if [ -n "$holder" ] && ! kill -0 "$holder" 2>/dev/null; then
121	      echo "STALE: holder pid $holder dead — reaping" >&2; rm -rf "$LOCK"; continue
122	    fi
123	    # No pidfile (old-cohort holder): reap only if NO live lake build AND the dir is >15 min old.
124	    if [ -z "$holder" ] && ! pgrep -f 'lake build AlgebraicJacobian' >/dev/null 2>&1 \
125	       && [ $(( $(date +%s) - $(stat -c %Y "$LOCK" 2>/dev/null || date +%s) )) -gt 900 ]; then
126	      echo "STALE: no live build, lock >15min old — reaping" >&2; rm -rf "$LOCK"; continue
127	    fi
128	  fi
129	  sleep 10
130	done
131	echo $$ > "$LOCK/pid" 2>/dev/null      # record holder so a later reaper can prove liveness via kill -0
132	# … lake build … ; rm -rf "$LOCK"      # release (rm -rf, not rmdir — the pidfile makes the dir non-empty)
133	```
134	
135	### 2a. THE RELEASE IS AS DANGEROUS AS THE REAP — check the pidfile before `rm -rf` (2026-07-28, run 0072)
136	
137	The acquire loop above is careful; the release (`rm -rf "$LOCK"`) is not, and that asymmetry
138	caused a real incident. **A lane removed the lock directory while its pidfile named a LIVE pid
139	belonging to another lane's build**, having printed `ALIVE` for that pid one line earlier.
140	
141	The mechanism is worth stating because nothing in the recipe warns about it. The offending lane
142	had legitimately acquired the lock, and then **its own shell was killed by a harness timeout
143	while it held it**. On the next turn it reasoned "the lock is mine and my holder is dead, so
144	release it" — but in the interval a *different* lane had acquired the lock, so the pid in the
145	file had never been its own. The lane was running the release branch on a belief about history
146	rather than on a reading of the file.
147	
148	> **Before `rm -rf "$LOCK"`, verify the pidfile still names YOUR pid.**
149	> `[ "$(cat "$LOCK/pid" 2>/dev/null)" = "$$" ] && rm -rf "$LOCK"`
150	> If it names anything else, the lock is not yours to release: say so and leave it alone.
151	
152	Two corollaries:
153	
154	* **"It was mine a minute ago" is not evidence**, especially when a harness can kill the shell
155	  between acquire and release. Every turn boundary is a window for another lane to take the lock.
156	* **Do not "repair" the mistake by re-creating the directory with the other lane's pid.**

---
name: lean-check
description: Build and check Lean in this workspace and read the errors — use Lean LSP MCP for fast proof-writing feedback, then run faithful kernel verification with `lake build` / `lake env lean`.
---

## Required proof loop

Load this skill before editing a Lean file. Before the first proof edit, invoke
at least one Lean LSP MCP query for the target (`lean_diagnostic_messages` or
`lean_goal`). After every proof edit, invoke diagnostics or the goal query again
before starting another tactic attempt. Use `lean_multi_attempt`, hover, and
search to investigate candidates instead of repeatedly launching a build.

Do not start iterative proof work with `lake build`: it is a slow, final-boundary
check. Use LSP for the edit loop and reserve `lake build` for the final session
validation (or when a kernel check is specifically needed). When LSP is
unavailable or crashes, record that in the report and use the narrowest fallback,
usually `lake env lean <file>` or a single module, rather than silently skipping
the check.

LSP is sufficient between edits and between separate obligations. Do not run a
module build after every proof or repeat a narrow build immediately before a
configured final build that covers the same files. At the final boundary, run
the configured build once and wait for it. Add an earlier narrow kernel check
only when LSP failed, the change crosses an interface LSP cannot validate, or a
specific elaboration/kernel question must be settled before continuing.

- During proof writing, prefer the Lean LSP MCP server for fast local feedback:
  inspect goals/diagnostics at the edited location before running a full build.
  This is the fastest loop for filling proofs.
- Treat LSP feedback as interactive guidance, not final verification. The
  faithful check is Lean's kernel via the project build: run the configured
  build command, `lake build <Module>`, or `lake env lean <file>` from the
  project root.
- Prefer the project's configured build command when validating a task. Otherwise
  use the narrowest faithful check that covers the changed file/module.
- Re-run after each change and repair failures you introduce.
- Read errors top-down — the first error often causes the cascade. For each,
  note the `file:line`, expected vs actual type, and remaining goal.
- A `sorry` left in place is an open obligation, not a success. Do not hide a
  hard obligation behind a new `sorry` unless a hint explicitly allows it.

## Fast LSP proving loop

The `lean-lsp` MCP server gives sub-second feedback — far faster than a build
(10–30s+). Drive proofs with it, then confirm with the kernel. Key tools:

- `lean_goal(file, line)` — the proof state at a line. Call before writing any
  tactic and after each one. Empty `goals_after` = that step closes the goal.
- `lean_diagnostic_messages(file)` — instant errors/warnings after every edit
  (`[]` = no errors, but *not* proof-complete — confirm with `lean_goal`).
- `lean_multi_attempt(file, line, snippets=[...])` — test 3–5 **single-line,
  indented** candidate tactics at once and see exactly which close the goal and
  why the others fail. The highest-leverage tool for filling a `sorry`.
- `lean_hover_info(file, line, col)` — type/signature/docs at an identifier
  (point at the first char). `lean_file_outline(file)` — declarations + line
  numbers without reading the whole file. `lean_run_code("#eval …")` — quick
  standalone `#check`/`#eval`/`#print`.

Core loop: `lean_goal` (what to prove) → search a premise (see the `leansearch`
skill: `lean_local_search` / `lean_leansearch`) → `lean_multi_attempt` (test
candidates) → edit with the winner → `lean_diagnostic_messages` (confirm) →
kernel-check the module at the end.

## Heavy builds — actually wait for them

Read the WHOLE build output, not just pass/fail: warnings (unused variables,
deprecations, `sorry` notices, unexpected recompiles) are actionable — fix the
ones your change introduced, and record pre-existing/toolchain ones as memory
or an inbox issue rather than scrolling past (see the `horizon` skill,
"Warnings are work").

A cold `lake build` (or one that recompiles Mathlib) can take many minutes. The
most common way a session ends on a wrong conclusion is **not waiting for the
build to finish**:

- Do **not** assume you will be "automatically notified" or "re-invoked" when a
  background build completes — whether that happens depends entirely on the
  mechanism you used. If unsure, run the build in the **foreground** and block on
  it until it exits, then read the exit code.
- If you run it in the background, you MUST actively wait: poll its status/output
  until there is a definitive exit code (a monitor / until-loop, re-reading the
  log), and only then conclude. A background job you started but walked away from
  is *not* done.
- Scope the build to the narrowest faithful check (`lake build <Module>` or
  `lake env lean <file>`) to keep the wait short; reserve the full project build
  for final validation.
- Never write your final report — or `complete` an inbox item, or mark a task
  done — while a build that affects your conclusion is still running. If the
  engine cannot wait long enough, say so explicitly under `## Issues` and leave
  the next action clear, rather than implying the proof checked.
- Before marking a task or roadmap item done/blocked/rejected, add a concise
  closing comment with the exact check command, result, relevant files, and any
  caveat. If a task has `roadmap_refs`, make sure the linked roadmap items end
  with a consistent status and their own sync/closing comment.

## When the LSP dies on big import files

The Lean LSP loads the full environment for the file you open. On a file whose
imports pull in most of Mathlib (a broad `import Mathlib` umbrella, or a module
that transitively imports one), that environment is huge and the LSP server can
run out of memory or time out and die. This is an LSP limitation, **not** a
proof error:

- Do not treat an LSP crash/timeout on such a file as a failure of your proof.
  Fall back to the kernel check: `lake build <Module>` or `lake env lean <file>`,
  which verifies faithfully without holding the whole environment interactively.
- Prefer opening the **narrowest** module in the LSP. Avoid pointing the LSP at
  umbrella/`import Mathlib`-style files just to get feedback; edit and inspect
  the specific module you are proving in instead.
- If the LSP has crashed, restart it (or just proceed with `lake build`) rather
  than repeatedly reopening the same giant file and getting the same crash.

283	    Sheaf.HModule (X.moduleKSheaf k) 1 ≃+ Additive (unitsReduction X U₀ U₁).ker :=

335	    ((Γ(X, U₀ ⊓ U₁)[ε])ˣ ⧸ cechCoboundaryUnits

344	      (resHom_overAlgebraMap_left k X U₀ U₁ a)
345	      (resHom_overAlgebraMap_right k X U₀ U₁ a))

348	overlap section by the structure constant: `[1 + b ε] ↦ [1 + (a·b) ε]`. -/
349	theorem mumfordScaling_mk_truncExpUnit (a : k) (b : Γ(X, U₀ ⊓ U₁)) :

371	  rw [h1AddEquivTruncExpCechKernel_smul_delta, h1AddEquivTruncExpCechKernel_delta,

9	/-!
10	# The tangent space of the Jacobian at the identity (W5-T5, the scalar-identity spine)
11	
12	The Wave-5 tangent statements phrased against the pinned representability datum
13	`(d : JacobianData C)` (roadmap `AJCR.w5-av.t5`), assembling the generic kit of
14	`Tangent/` into the two forms Wave 5 actually consumes:
15	
16	```
17	Dual κ(e) (m_e/m_e²)  ≃  T_e(d.J)  ≃  ker (Pic⁰(Spec k[ε]) →* Pic⁰(Spec k))
18	```
19	
20	and, under the **one** remaining numerical input, the frozen scalar identity
21	`dim_κ(e) m_e/m_e² = genus C` together with its additive consequence
22	`m_e/m_e² ≃+ H¹(C, 𝒪_C)`.
23	
24	## The scalar-identity-first discipline (w5-worksheet D6), and what it buys
25	
26	The W12 lesson recorded in the worksheet is that dimension transport must go
27	through **one** `finrank` identity, followed by **one** non-canonical `≃+` — not
28	through a chain of additive equivalences each carrying its own linearity
29	bookkeeping. This file is that discipline made structural:
30	
31	* `JacobianData.tangentSpaceEquivPic0Kernel` is the representability leg,
32	  unconditional and sorry-free. It is a bijection of **sets**; it deliberately
33	  does *not* claim to transport dimension (a bare `Equiv` cannot).
34	* `JacobianData.finrank_cotangentSpaceDual_eq_genus` isolates the numerical
35	  content as a **hypothesis** `hdim`. That hypothesis is what the T3/T4 chain must
36	  deliver.
37	* `JacobianData.nonempty_cotangentSpace_addEquiv_h1` then produces the additive
38	  equivalence from the count, once.
39	
40	So the Wave-5 tangent keystone is, at HEAD, reduced to a statement about the
41	`ε`-kernel of `pic0Functor` — **but note precisely which statement**. The
42	`ε`-kernel *bijection* above is not enough on its own: it is a bijection of sets,
43	and `finrank` does not transport along one. What `hdim` needs is the **semilinear
44	comparison** — an additive equivalence plus the intertwining law across
45	`κ(e) ≃+* k` — fed through `finrank_eq_of_addEquiv_of_bijective_smul` (proved
46	below, unconditionally). Stating T3/T4's target as a bare kernel bijection would
47	leave the count unreachable; this is the same residue the AJC sibling isolated as
48	`semilinearComparison_cotangentSpaceDual_h1Cok`. See inbox I-0513.
49	
50	Note that the
51	identity point of `d.J` needs no rationality hypothesis: it is the image of the
52	group-object unit, hence a section, hence automatically `k`-rational
53	(`bijective_algebraMap_residueField_of_section`).
54	
55	## Main declarations
56	
57	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.identitySection` — the `k`-rational identity
58	  point of `d.J`, with `identitySection_isSection`.
59	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.tangentSpaceCotangentDual` — `T_0(d.J)` is the
60	  `κ(e)`-linear dual of the cotangent space at the identity.
61	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.tangentSpaceEquivPic0Kernel` — `T_0(d.J)` is
62	  the `ε`-kernel of `pic0Functor C` (the representability leg, applied).
63	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.cotangentSpaceDual_equiv_pic0Kernel` — the two
64	  composed: the cotangent dual at the identity *is* the `ε`-kernel.
65	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.finiteDimensional_cotangentSpace` — the
66	  cotangent space at the identity is finite-dimensional (from
67	  `d.locallyOfFiniteType`).
68	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.finrank_eq_of_addEquiv_of_bijective_smul` —
69	  **unconditional**: `finrank` transports across a scalar *bijection* given an
70	  additive equivalence and the intertwining law. The bridge that makes the count
71	  reachable at all.
72	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.finrank_cotangentSpaceDual_eq_genus` /
73	  `nonempty_cotangentSpace_addEquiv_h1` — the frozen scalar identity and its
74	  additive consequence, each conditional on the T3/T4 semilinear comparison.
75	
76	Reference: Kleiman, "The Picard scheme", §5 Thm. 5.11 (arXiv:math/0504020);
77	Milne, "Abelian varieties", Prop. 2.1.
78	-/

167	/-! ## The frozen scalar identity, and the bridge T3/T4 must actually cross
168	
169	Everything above is unconditional. What follows carries the numerical input as an
170	explicit hypothesis, named once:
171	
172	```
173	hdim : Module.finrank κ(e) (m_e/m_e²) = genus C
174	```
175	
176	Keeping it a hypothesis rather than a `sorry` is the w5-worksheet §0(4) rule
177	(never register a staged fact).
178	
179	**What `hdim` needs, stated precisely — the `ε`-kernel bijection alone is NOT
180	enough.** `tangentSpaceEquivPic0Kernel` is a bijection of *sets* (it says so on
181	its own docstring) and a bare `Equiv` does not determine `finrank`. So T3/T4's
182	kernel computation does not by itself give `hdim`: additionally required is an
183	**additive** equivalence together with the intertwining law across the
184	residue-field bijection `κ(e) → k`, because the two sides are modules over
185	genuinely different rings — neither `LinearEquiv.finrank_eq` nor a
186	`restrictScalars` argument applies.
187	
188	`finrank_eq_of_addEquiv_of_bijective_smul` below is exactly that bridge, and it
189	is unconditional. With it in hand the residual obligation on T3/T4 is the
190	**semilinear comparison**: a scalar bijection `i`, an additive equivalence `j`
191	from `Dual κ(e) (m_e/m_e²)` to `H¹(C,𝒪)`, and `j (r • x) = i r • j x`. That is
192	the honest target to state T3/T4 against — and it is the same residue the AJC
193	sibling isolated (`semilinearComparison_cotangentSpaceDual_h1Cok`), which is why
194	porting the generic kit without this bridge would have left the count
195	unreachable. Found by fresh-context review; see inbox I-0513. -/
196	
197	/-- **`finrank` across a scalar bijection** (the linearity bridge the Wave-5
198	count needs, and the reason the `ε`-kernel *set* bijection is insufficient on its
199	own). If `i : R → R'` is a bijection of scalars, `j : M ≃+ M₁` an additive
200	equivalence, and the two intertwine (`j (r • m) = i r • j m`), then `M` and `M₁`
201	have equal `finrank` over their respective rings.
202	
203	`i` need only be a **bijection**, not a ring homomorphism, and the module
204	structures live over genuinely different rings — which is precisely the situation
205	of the Kleiman §5 Thm. 5.11 count, comparing a `κ(e)`-dimension with a
206	`k`-dimension across `κ(e) ≃+* k`. Mathlib has this at the level of
207	`Module.rank` (`rank_eq_of_equiv_equiv`) but not in `finrank` form; this is the
208	`Module.finrank = toNat ∘ Module.rank` unfolding of it. -/
209	theorem finrank_eq_of_addEquiv_of_bijective_smul

12	original sections, naturally in the **open**. This file supplies the other direction — the one
13	the `ε`-kernel computation actually spends — namely that the section map induced by the `ε ↦ 0`
14	test-object morphism **is** `TrivSqZeroExt.fst`:

17	relSectionsMap C k[ε] k W ∘ dualNumberSections C  =  (· ⊗ₜ 1) ∘ TrivSqZeroExt.fst
18	```

21	statement with `TruncExpCech.unitsFst` (`Over.relSectionsMapUnits_dualNumberSectionsUnits`).
22	
23	## Why this needs a `scoped` algebra instance, and where it comes from
24	
25	The tree's coefficient-direction tool `AlgebraicGeometry.relSectionsMap`
26	(`Cohomology/RelativeSectionsLinear.lean`) binds `[Algebra R R'] [IsScalarTower k R R']`, and at
27	`R := k[ε]`, `R' := k` neither is found by instance search.
28	
29	**Both exist upstream** — `TrivSqZeroExt.algebraBase` and the `IsScalarTower` immediately after it
30	(`Mathlib/Algebra/TrivSqZeroExt/Basic.lean:890, :897`) — but `algebraBase` is deliberately **not an
31	instance**, because (mathlib's own comment) it "creates a different
32	`Algebra (TrivSqZeroExt R' M) (TrivSqZeroExt R' M)` instance from `TrivSqZeroExt.algebra'`". So
33	`epsAlgebra`/`epsIsScalarTower` below are `scoped` **re-exposures**, not constructions: instances
34	only inside `namespace TruncExpCech.EpsilonReduction`, which a consumer opens explicitly, never in
35	ambient search. With them the whole landed `relSectionsMap` API applies unchanged —
36	`relSectionsMap_pullback`, `relSectionsMap_overAlgebraMap`, `relSectionsMap_resHom` — which is why
37	this file is short: the geometry was already proved, and so was the algebra.
38	
39	**An earlier version of this docstring said mathlib "has none" and justified `scoped` by a diamond
40	with `Algebra k k`. Both were wrong** (reviewer finding, inbox `I-0634`; a clash between *different*
41	types is impossible, and the real clash is at `Algebra (tsze) (tsze)`). The pattern is `I-0567`'s —
42	*present upstream but deliberately not an instance*, like a `private` name — not absent
43	infrastructure.

45	The identification itself is then a `rfl`: with `epsAlgebra` in scope,
46	`algebraMap k[ε] k = TrivSqZeroExt.fst` **definitionally** (`algebraMap_eps_eq_fst`), so
47	`relSectionsMap_overAlgebraMap` computes the reduction directly and the `ε` component dies
48	because `algebraMap k[ε] k ε = 0`.

52	Two `rw` walls, both the elided-restriction-argument family recorded at
53	`Tangent/TwoChartNormalize.lean` and `informal/w5-t4-worksheet.md` §6.10(3), and both worked
54	around the same way — never fight them, close by `exact`:
55	
56	* `map_add` of `relSectionsMap` will not `rw` into the goal, because the goal mentions
57	  `(C ⊗ overSpec k R).left` where the lemma mentions `relCurve C R` (equal by `rfl`, not
58	  syntactically). Apply it as a **term** via `RingHom.map_add` and `.trans`.
59	* the final `a + 0 = a` likewise resists `rw [add_zero]`; `exact add_zero _` closes it.
60	
61	## Main declarations
62	
63	* `TruncExpCech.EpsilonReduction.epsAlgebra` / `epsIsScalarTower` — the scoped instances.
64	* `TruncExpCech.EpsilonReduction.algebraMap_eps_eq_fst` — `algebraMap k[ε] k` is `fst` (`rfl`).
65	* `AlgebraicGeometry.Over.relSectionsMap_sectionsBaseChange_tmul` — the reduction on a pure
66	  tensor.

68	* `AlgebraicGeometry.Over.relSectionsMapUnits_dualNumberSectionsUnits` — the unit form, which

70	
71	Reference: Kleiman, "The Picard scheme", §5 Thm. 5.11 (arXiv:math/0504020);
72	`informal/w5-t4-worksheet.md` §6.13.
